titre: “Donatello chez les fauves” (Donatello Among the Wild Beasts): A Movement Named by a Single Sentence
accroche: The name of the Fauves comes from a critic's joke about a small marble bust, published in a newspaper in 1905.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1905, the Salon d'Automne, held in Paris, brings together in Room VII a group of young painters gathered around Henri Matisse, whose canvases use bold, unmixed colors: Henri Manguin, André Derain, Maurice de Vlaminck and others. At the center of the room stand two sculptures by Albert Marque, classical in style, including a small marble bust.

The critic Louis Vauxcelles visits the exhibition and reviews it in *Gil Blas* on October 17, 1905, in the daily's supplement. The passage quoted by Wikipedia opens on the room: “An ultra-bright room, with daring ones, extremists, whose intentions have to be deciphered.” Of Room VII, he writes: “The candor of these busts is surprising amid the orgy of pure tones: Donatello among the wild beasts...”

## What the Sentence Targets

Read closely, the sentence comments first on a sculpture, not on the painting. The “Donatello” is the bust; the “wild beasts” are the canvases and the painters around it. Larousse places the bust at the center of Room VII, amid a group of young painters around Matisse: the sentence comments on this proximity. Vauxcelles is amused by the contrast between a well-behaved work, classical in style, and walls saturated with pure color. Donatello is only a comparison: the busts are the work of a living sculptor, Albert Marque.

Yet the phrase becomes a hit. Larousse writes that we owe the term “fauves” to Vauxcelles, and sees in it a quip that will start a school, from which the term “Fauvism” quickly takes shape. A movement is thus named by a critic's remark tossed off about a sculpture placed in the middle of its painters.

## A Name More Durable Than the Movement

The twist lies in duration. Fauvism as a group is brief: the same Larousse article notes that it died of its own intensity only four years after the Salon d'Automne of 1905. The name, for its part, has endured, and it is the one art history still uses for these painters.

Vauxcelles left history another label: he is also credited with the word “cubes,” used in *Gil Blas* on November 14, 1908, about Georges Braque. Two movements, two critics' words, three years apart.

carte.punch: The Fauves owe their name to a joke about a marble bust.
carte.idee: In 1905, at the Salon d'Automne, the critic Louis Vauxcelles sees a classical bust by Albert Marque amid the canvases of Matisse and Derain and writes: “Donatello among the wild beasts.” The word passes to the painters and names the movement.

quiz.question: What does the formula “Donatello chez les fauves” (Donatello among the wild beasts) refer to in Vauxcelles's sentence?
choix: A painting by Matisse done in the manner of the Renaissance
A work by Donatello lent to the Salon d'Automne of 1905
The Salon jury, compared to a Renaissance master
A classical bust by Albert Marque, surrounded by colorful canvases
quiz.explication: Vauxcelles compares Albert Marque's classically styled bust, placed at the center of Room VII, to the art of Donatello, and the “wild beasts” refer to the canvases and the painters around it. Donatello appears only as a comparison, and the sentence targets neither a Matisse painting nor the jury.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which newspaper and on what date does Vauxcelles publish the formula “Donatello chez les fauves” (Donatello among the wild beasts)?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The sentence appears in the supplement of Gil Blas of October 17, 1905, the day after the critic's visit to the Salon d'Automne, in Room VII, where the young painters were exhibiting.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other word does Vauxcelles go on to coin, and about whom?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Vauxcelles uses the word “cubes” in Gil Blas of November 14, 1908, about Georges Braque, three years after naming the Fauves.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long did Fauvism last as a group movement, according to Larousse?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Larousse writes that Fauvism died of its own intensity only four years after the Salon d'Automne of 1905, although the name itself has lasted.
